title: The Leading Column Must Be in the Predicate
description: A composite index can't seek when the query filters only its second column; index the column you actually search on. Why it matters: composite indexes are frequently added for one query and then silently fail to help a different, very similar-looking query -- this is exactly why, and it's a common source of confusion in code review.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a mistake that's genuinely easy to make and genuinely easy to miss: a composite index exists, the column you're filtering by is technically *inside* that index — and yet the index provides essentially no help at all, because of where in the column order it sits.

The setup: there's one nonclustered index, `IX_Orders_Cust_Prod`, built on `(CustomerId, ProductId)` — two columns, in that order. A report needs "all orders for product 42," so it filters with `WHERE ProductId = 42`. `ProductId` is right there in the index — surely that should help? But the query still scans the whole table, getting no benefit whatsoever from an index that contains the exact column being searched.

The mental model that unlocks this is thinking of a composite index the way you'd think of a phone book sorted by **last name, then first name**. If you want to look up "everyone named Smith," that sort order is perfect — jump straight to the Smith section. But if you want to look up "everyone whose first name is John," regardless of last name — that same phone book gives you almost no help at all. Johns are scattered across every single letter of the alphabet, one per last-name section, in no particular grouped order relative to each other. Yes, the information "is this person named John" is technically present in the book — but the book isn't organized in a way that lets you *find* all the Johns without essentially reading the entire thing cover to cover.

That's exactly the situation with `(CustomerId, ProductId)`: the index is sorted first by `CustomerId`, and only *within* each customer's block, sorted by `ProductId`. Product 42's orders are scattered across every single customer's individual block — one entry per customer who happened to order product 42 — with no overall grouping by product at all. To find "every order of product 42," SQL Server would have to check inside every single customer's section of the index individually, looking for a `ProductId = 42` entry, which is essentially just as much work as reading the entire index start to finish. There's no useful shortcut, because the *first* thing the index is sorted by — the thing that lets you jump to a specific starting point — is `CustomerId`, and this query never mentions `CustomerId` at all.

This is the concept of the **leading column** (sometimes called the "left-most column"): the first column in a composite index's definition is the only one that, by itself, lets SQL Server directly seek into the structure and jump to a starting point. Every column *after* the leading column is only useful for narrowing things down *within* a group that's already been narrowed down by everything before it. If your query's filter doesn't include the leading column at all, the index can't be seeked using that filter — it can, at best, only be scanned (read start to finish, checking each entry), which usually isn't any better than just scanning the underlying table directly, and sometimes is worse because the engine then also has to go do a lookup back to the main table for the other columns it needs.

The fix, in this case, is straightforward: if `ProductId` is genuinely something you search by on its own (independent of any particular customer), you need a *different* index where `ProductId` is the leading column — either a brand-new index on `(ProductId)` (possibly with an `INCLUDE` for other needed columns), or, if there's also a common query pattern that filters by both product and customer together, a composite index like `(ProductId, CustomerId)`. The existing `(CustomerId, ProductId)` index isn't wrong or useless — it's just built for a different question ("this customer's orders of any product"), not the question this particular report is asking ("this product's orders across any customer").

Why does this matter in practice? Composite indexes very often get built to support one specific, well-known query — a dashboard, a common lookup — and then, months or years later, someone writes a *new* query that happens to filter by one of that index's non-leading columns, sees that the column is "in an index," and assumes it'll be fast, without realizing that column order makes all the difference. This is one of the most common causes of "there's an index, why is this scanning?" confusion, and recognizing "is the column I'm filtering by actually the *leading* column of this index?" as the very first thing to check is an essential diagnostic habit.

A good way to stress-test your understanding of this lesson is to imagine three different reports against the same `(CustomerId, ProductId)` index and predict, before checking, whether each one can seek efficiently: "all orders for customer 100" (yes — filters on the leading column alone); "all orders for customer 100, product 42" (yes — filters on both columns, in the order the index expects); "all orders for product 42, across any customer" (no — this is exactly the lesson's example, since it skips the leading column entirely). If you can correctly predict all three without running them, you've internalized the core idea: seekability depends on whether your filter includes the *leading* column of whatever index you're hoping to use, not merely on whether the column you care about happens to be present somewhere in that index's definition. This is genuinely one of the fastest mental checks you can run when looking at any execution plan that surprises you with a scan instead of a seek — check the index's column order against the actual WHERE clause, column by column, starting from the left.

One more thing worth knowing: SQL Server can sometimes still use a non-leading column of an index for a scan (reading the whole index instead of the whole table, since the index is usually narrower), which can be marginally cheaper than a full table scan if the index is much smaller than the table -- but this is a consolation prize, not a real fix, and you should still build a properly-ordered index for any query pattern you expect to run repeatedly.

## Scenario
`Orders` has one nonclustered index, `IX_Orders_Cust_Prod` on `(CustomerId, ProductId)`. A report filters by product alone: `WHERE ProductId = 42`. Even though `ProductId` is *in* the index, the query scans.

## Why it's slow
An index is a sorted list keyed **left to right**. `(CustomerId, ProductId)` is ordered by `CustomerId` first; rows for `ProductId = 42` are scattered across every `CustomerId` group. SQL Server can only **seek** on a **prefix** of the key — here that prefix must start with `CustomerId`. With no `CustomerId` predicate, the index isn't seekable for this query, so SQL Server scans.

## Not the same as key *order* for a range
Choosing which column leads for a multi-predicate or `ORDER BY` query (covered separately) is about *ordering the seek*. This lesson is simpler and more absolute: if the **leading** column never appears in the `WHERE`, the index can't be seeked at all.

## The fix
Add an index whose **leading** key is the column you actually filter on: `IX_Orders_Prod` on `(ProductId)` (INCLUDE the columns you select to make it covering). Now `WHERE ProductId = 42` seeks straight to the ~200 matching rows.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, ProductId, Total FROM Orders WHERE ProductId = 42;
hints: ProductId is the SECOND key of IX_Orders_Cust_Prod. Can an index seek on its second column alone?
An index seek needs a left-to-right prefix of the key. The prefix here starts with CustomerId, which the query doesn't filter on.
Create an index that leads with ProductId: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Prod ON Orders(ProductId) INCLUDE(CustomerId, Total);
